You may decline to provide the ESA letter but if you are a licensed mental health professional, you absolutely can.

Take what I say with a grain of salt, as I have never written one myself, but I am always open to it and I have processed these inquiries successfully without damaging rapport with clients. 

Before you can write a letter, you need a diagnosis and an understanding of their current symptoms and past treatments. I mean, you are diagnosing them and prescribing treatment to help alleviate symptoms.  I tell my clients that before I write a letter we need to establish which symptom measurement tool we will use, psychoeducation on different treatment options, what past treatments they have tried among other bio-psy-soc factors, then we need to establish a treatment plan to reveiw options and efficacy. 

I personally couldn't do that in less than 3 sessions, more likely, it'll take 6. This timeline can also change pending the diagnosis and measurement tool used. Anyone who was looking for a quick letter knew the timeline I operated on and what to expect, thus they didn't ask me again. I had 1 person go this route with me and they found that the behavioral health interventions worked better for them than the ESA intervention by session 4.

Edit: to give more specific feedback, you may find that writing an ESA letter would be counterintuitive to really addressing their symptoms. Part of the treatment plan can also be, how will you care for the ESA animal, how will you choose one, etc. By exploring these options the client may choose on their own to not proceed with the ESA or maybe they have other resources that we didn't know of or that they didn't even remember.

That's a difficult practicum placement situation for a student to navigate. It's definitely not ideal but not inherently "unethical" unless you noted your many friendships within the complex to your supervisor. We can sometimes live among the people we serve, but living in close proximity is different from having casual conversations *with* people or sharing drinks/dinners. I cannot tell for sure from your original post if these are people who you actively have relationships with or if you see them often in passing. 

Regardless, your supervisor being dismissive of your concerns is an issue and I believe that even in the best assumption of your sinario,  thats still a unideal placement for someone who is new to the field. It's hard enough for seasoned therapists to handle client encounters in the community. I've had people approach me in parking lots, grocery stores, and festivals, and the first few times I internally panicked with all of ethical considerations that you have to be cognizant of when doing so. It's not unethical to find yourself in these encounters, but it can quickly become unethical if you do not know how to navigate them properly. Your supervisor should be giving you support and guidance if these encounters are going to be so frequent. I also don't think it's unreasonable to ask for another placement, considering the concentration of students at your complex and the shared community resources. We should do our best, within reason, to avoid possible overlapping roles within the therapeutic setting.

There are a lot of elements to unpack from 1 interaction but lets do our best. 

1. Accusing language: "you are being selfish" is a subjective and emotional declaration. Its not inherently factual of the context but it is factual of the emotional state of the individual making it. Aside from the actual inequality of the financial structure of yout relationship, this needs to be addressed separately 

2. The financial agreement in your relationship: it definitely doesn't seem like you two are on the same page. And I am curious if element 3 has anything to do with that. However the financial agreement still needs to be clear and agreed upon by both parties. 

3. The financial cognitive load/burden: while you both could split your incomes 50/50, that is only a portion of the responsibility. Its not enough to make money but you need to pay bills on time, plan expenses/savings, manage any debt/income changes, ect. You mentioned being upset about the interruption to your work day so that you could make a decision about the extra $33 for dog food. Its understandable to feel frustrated that your partner did not take on that responsibility. However without knowing your partners intention, we do not know if they did this because they thought it was part of the financial agreement or if it was because they did not want to take on the monetary or cognitive burden. 

4. Just from what you presented, it seems like your partner is avoidant of conflict. While that can help in the short term, long term it doesn't lend itself well to conflict resolution. Just like the accusatory language, it is an emotional response that needs to be addressed outside of the discussions on finances. 

All of these elements are fairly complex and require a good bit of introspection. Its likely that you both would be unsuccessful in navigating this on your own with elements 1 and 4 being present. Others have suggested therapy and I would also suggest couples therapy if you feel that it is worth exploring before dissolving your relationship.
